rashi:a1.1: Three fields and two furrows: the field in which the grave was, and a field on this side and a field on that side. If the custom of the people of the valley is to plow their fields east and west, it makes the field to the east and the field to the west a beit haperas; and if they plow north and south, [it makes] the one to the north and the one to the south a beit haperas, since there the plow rolled the earth of the beit haperas and the bones. But not to all four directions, since it is not the custom to plow lengthwise and crosswise. And those two fields themselves are not entirely a beit haperas, but only the measure of two furrows, a furrow for this one and a furrow for that one. But the field in which the grave is is entirely impure, since we do not know in which place in it the grave was. And therefore it makes a full furrow on each side, since perhaps the grave was at one of its two ends, and from there it went into the neighboring field a full furrow; for this is the measure of the plowing of a grave, as so the Sages estimated: over a full furrow the bones are liable to be rolled along by the plow.
rashi:a2.1: The teruma of both of them is teruma: since both of them have a share in it.
rashi:a3.1: The teruma of neither of them is teruma: even that of the first, since once the second went back and separated teruma, he revealed his mind that he is not content with the teruma of the first, and so the first is one who separates teruma without [his partner’s] consent; and likewise the second.
rashi:a3.3: And if not: for example, he separated stingily, then the teruma of the second is teruma. And according to Rabbi Akiva, either way it is not teruma; and our mishna too states it without qualification. Therefore it is Rabbi Akiva.
rashi:a6.1: To include an unwitting one as an intentional one: and below, in the second chapter (Temurah 17a), it explains it: he intended to substitute a black animal and substituted a white one. With regard to consecrated items, this is not consecrated, since it is a mistaken consecration; but with regard to substitution, it is consecrated.
rashi:a7.1: Mishna. Only an animal: “he substitutes an animal for an animal.”
rashi:a7.2: Items consecrated for Temple maintenance do not effect substitution: since with regard to substitution “offering” is written, and items consecrated for Temple maintenance are not called an offering, as the Gemara explains.
rashi:a8.1: Rabbi Shimon said, etc.: since he holds that items consecrated for Temple maintenance are called an offering, therefore we derive that they do not effect substitution only from here: But wasn’t the animal tithe included in the category of all consecrated animals, which effect substitution, as it is written: “And if he substitutes at all,” etc. (Leviticus 27:10)? Why was it singled out, in that it is written with regard to it that it effects substitution: “And if he substitutes at all,” etc. [Leviticus 27:33]? Just as the tithe is an individual offering that effects substitution, so too every individual offering effects substitution, excluding communal offerings; for the tithe does not exist in partnership, as we say in the last chapter of Bekhorot (56b): “Shall be yours,” and not of partnership.
rashi:a10.1: Gemara. Offering: “And if it is an animal of which men bring an offering,” etc., and after it is written: “He shall not alter it.”
rashi:a11.1: If “offering,” I would understand, etc.: this refers to [the passage of] slaughtering outside [the Temple]. And this “if” is the language of Torat Kohanim, as we say in many places: “Or is it not,” etc. Concerning slaughtering outside, [the baraita] earlier expounded this same word “offering” for another exposition, as it teaches: “Offering”: for an offering one is liable to karet outside, and one is not liable to karet for non-sacred animals [slaughtered] inside. And on this it teaches: If “offering”; that is to say, if we expound this “offering” in this way, it would imply even items consecrated for Temple maintenance, etc. And some say [it is “or”] because it is written there: “or who slaughters”; but that is not so.
rashi:a11.2: Items consecrated for Temple maintenance: ordinarily they are blemished and are not fit for the Tent of Meeting; nevertheless they are called an offering.
rashi:a13.1: According to Rabbi Shimon: of our mishna, they are called an offering, and therefore he excludes them by the juxtaposition with the animal tithe, and not from “offering.”
rashi:a14.1: They are not called “an offering to the Lord”: for that would imply an offering without qualification; but as it is [“the Lord’s offering”], it does not imply an offering without qualification.
rashi:a15.1: This is the reading: The Sages taught: “He shall not inquire,” etc. Another version reads [in Rabbi Ḥanina’s answer]: This is Rabbi and that is Rabbi Shimon; according to Rabbi Shimon they are called an offering, according to Rabbi they are not called an offering. And according to this version we explain that in the mishna there is no dispute, but it is all Rabbi Shimon: that which it teaches, “Items consecrated for Temple maintenance do not effect substitution,” is not derived from “offering,” but Rabbi Shimon states it and then explains the reason. Therefore one cannot say: This is Rabbi Shimon and that is the Rabbis. For this version, this is the reading: What is [the source of] Rabbi, and what is [the source of] Rabbi Shimon? As it is taught: “He shall not inquire whether it is good or bad,” etc.
rashi:a15.2: Why is it stated: this verse with regard to the tithe? And wasn’t it already stated: “He shall not alter it,” etc., which implies that all consecrated animals effect substitution, and the tithe is included?
rashi:a16.1: And offerings of Temple maintenance: and this entire baraita is Rabbi Shimon, who holds that items consecrated for Temple maintenance are called an offering, and Rabbi Shimon goes on to explain the reason. And even according to the first version, this is certainly all Rabbi Shimon, as it teaches: “The verse states: He shall not inquire,” etc.; that is to say, it is for this that substitution was written again with regard to the tithe: to juxtapose all other consecrated animals to it, as Rabbi Shimon says.
rashi:a17.1: And an item of obligation: it is explained below what this excludes.
rashi:a17.2: And an item that is not in partnership: as I explained above: “Shall be yours,” and not of partnership.
tosafot:a1.1: Three fields of two furrows: Rashi explained: the field in which the grave was, and a field on this side and a field on that side; if the custom of the valley is to plow their fields from east to west, it makes the field to the east and the field to the west a beit haperas, and if they plow north and south, they make the field to the north and to the south a beit haperas. These are Rashi’s words. And this reason works well for the Rabbis. But what Rashi explained for Rabbi Eliezer does not seem right, for he explained that all four fields around his beit haperas are a beit haperas and their earth renders impure. And what is the reason for this? If they plowed from east to west, why should north and south be impure; and if they plowed from north to south, why should east and west be impure? Therefore it seems [correct] to explain: Rabbi Eliezer says that one beit haperas creates another beit haperas, meaning that whatever is plowed from the beit haperas into another field next to it makes it a beit haperas; and likewise if it was plowed from that second field into a third, and from the third into a fourth, and so on forever: they all make one another a beit haperas.
tosafot:a2.1: The mishna is Rabbi Akiva, as we learned: Partners who separated teruma one after the other, Rabbi Eliezer says: The teruma of both of them is teruma: since both of them have a share in it. And as for what we exclude from “you,” and not partners, that concerns [a case where] their whole teruma is not teruma; but part of this one’s teruma and part of that one’s is teruma.
tosafot:a3.1: Rabbi Akiva says: The teruma of neither of them is teruma: Rashi explained: even that of the first, since once the second went back and separated teruma, he revealed his mind that he is not content with the teruma of the first, and he is one who separates teruma without consent; and likewise the second. These are Rashi’s words. But this does not seem right, for this is not like “nor a substitute after a substitute,” since there the first is a substitute and the second is not a substitute. Therefore it seems [correct] to explain likewise here, that the first is teruma and not the second. And it is difficult, for in the third chapter of tractate Terumot [mishna 3] we learned: Partners who separated teruma, Rabbi Akiva says: The teruma of both of them is teruma; and the Sages say: If the first separated of the measure, etc. If so, Rabbi Akiva contradicts Rabbi Akiva. And it seems to the Ri that our passage deals with where they gave each other permission to separate teruma; therefore the teruma of the first is teruma according to Rabbi Akiva, as he separated with his fellow’s consent, and the second’s is nothing, since he gave his fellow permission to separate and he had already separated. And Rabbi Eliezer holds that the teruma of both of them is teruma, since they revealed their minds that each one is content with his fellow’s teruma [the printed text adds “not” here in parentheses, marking it for deletion]. But there [in Terumot] it is where they did not give each other permission to separate; therefore each one separated his own portion with his own intent, and therefore the teruma of both of them is partially teruma.
gershom:a1.1: One beit haperas does not create another beit haperas: for a field in which a grave was plowed is a beit haperas, and the whole field is of uncertain impurity; and we do not say that all the fields around it are impure lest a bone the size of a barley grain went out of it and entered those fields. Rather, that field alone in which [the grave] was plowed is impure, and the rest are pure. And according to the Rabbis, how far does the area of a beit haperas reach? When Rav Dimi came, he said that Reish Lakish said: Three fields. If the impurity was in the middle one, then the measure of two furrows outside the middle field, a full furrow on this side and a full furrow on that side in the outer fields, is a beit haperas. And he did not want to say five fields, that is to say, that on all four sides of that field [one hundred cubits] would be a beit haperas, but only two furrows, a furrow on this side and a furrow on that side. And this is the reason: [because he took the way of plowing,] and a person does not usually plow his field lengthwise and crosswise.
gershom:a2.1: A full furrow is one hundred cubits: that is an area of four se’a, for one hundred by [one hundred] is an area for sowing four se’a, as we derive from the courtyard of the Tabernacle, where one hundred by fifty is an area of two se’a. (Rabbi Yosei says: five.) And Rabbi Yosei’s reason was not explained to us.
gershom:a3.1: And there is no teruma after teruma: for one does not separate two [great] terumot from one pile.
gershom:a4.1: Partners who separated teruma one after the other: from one pile.
gershom:a5.1: Rabbi Eliezer says: The teruma of both of them is teruma: [because] each one separates by his own intent. [Rabbi Yosei says:] If the first separated of the measure that the Sages stated: a generous eye separates one-fortieth, an average one one-fiftieth, a stingy eye one-sixtieth. [The bracketed “Rabbi Yosei says” is in the printed text of Rabbeinu Gershom; the daf reads “the Rabbis say.”]
gershom:a6.1: The teruma of the second is not teruma: since the first already exempted it.
gershom:a7.1: Since substitution is stated only with regard to an animal: as it is written: “And if it is an animal of which men bring an offering to the Lord, all that any man gives of it,” etc., “he shall not alter it,” etc.
gershom:a8.1: Rabbi Shimon explains what the reason is that they do not effect substitution: [for the tithe was included in the category of every animal, and why was it singled out? To juxtapose, etc.]
gershom:a9.1: [And isn’t it taught:] If “offering,” as it is written: “Or who slaughters it outside the camp, and has not brought it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting to present it as an offering to the Lord,” I would understand that even for items consecrated for Temple maintenance one would be liable for slaughtering outside, though these were not consecrated to be sacrificed themselves but for their value.
gershom:a10.1: This is not difficult: this is Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi], who below interprets “why was the tithe singled out” for a different exposition, and not to exclude offerings of Temple maintenance. Evidently he holds that items consecrated for Temple maintenance are not called an offering, and no verse was needed to exclude them. And this is Rabbi Shimon, who holds that the tithe was singled out for this, to exclude them; evidently, because he holds that they are called an offering. [Rabbeinu Gershom reads “Rabbi” here where the daf reads “the Rabbis.”]
gershom:a11.1: And according to Rabbi they are not called an offering? But isn’t it written, etc.: according to this version, it now says: What is [the source of] Rabbi, and what is [the source of] Rabbi Shimon? As the Sages taught, etc. And according to the other version, which says: According to the Rabbis it is not called an offering, it holds that the anonymous mishna, which teaches: Items consecrated for Temple maintenance do not effect substitution, is the Rabbis, since they did not need a verse to exclude them, because they hold that they are not called an offering; and Rabbi Shimon, who says: But wasn’t the tithe included, needs to exclude them from the tithe, evidently because he holds that they are called an offering. And it says: And according to the Rabbis are they not called an offering? But isn’t it written, etc. For everything is implied [by “he shall not alter it”], that they effect substitution. And according to this version it does not ask: What is [the source of] Rabbi and what is [the source of] Rabbi Shimon, but begins the baraita that teaches: The Sages taught: “He shall not inquire,” etc.
rashi:b2.1: Rabbi says: Why was the tithe singled out now: for Rabbi holds that it was not needed for all these. For an individual offering is derived from “he shall not substitute,” which is singular language; and an altar offering is derived from “offering”; evidently Rabbi holds that items consecrated for Temple maintenance are not called an offering. And as for an item of obligation, from which Rabbi Shimon excludes a burnt offering that comes from surplus, Rabbi holds that surplus goes to communal gift offerings, and from the first clause of the mishna we derive that there is no substitution for the community. And partnership too [is excluded] from “he shall not substitute,” singular language.
rashi:b2.2: Since the tithe was singled out to be discussed with regard to substitution of its name: as it is written earlier: “And all the tithe,” and we include from “all” that if he called the tenth ninth and the eleventh tenth, both are consecrated; and that is substitution of its name. Therefore it was necessary to write also: “And if he substitutes it at all,” to discuss substitution of its body: if he set a non-sacred animal beside the tithe and said: This is like this, it is seized as a substitute. For had [the verse] not written it, I would say it does not effect substitution, as we say below: an item that was included in a category and was singled out to be discussed with a new matter, which is the novelty of substitution of its name, which does not exist in all consecrated animals; and I would say: you have in it only its novelty, substitution of its name, but not substitution of its body. For this reason the verse repeated it, and it was singled out to be discussed with substitution of its name and of its body.
rashi:b3.1: Substitution of its name is sacrificed: as we say at the end of Bekhorot (61a): “The herd” comes to include the eleventh as a peace offering.
rashi:b3.2: Substitution of its body is not sacrificed: as we say earlier in our chapter (Temurah 5b): [the tithe] derives “passing,” “passing” from the firstborn, and with regard to the firstborn it is written: “They” [are sacred]: they are sacrificed, and their substitutes are not sacrificed.
rashi:b3.3: Substitution of its name is redeemed: for it is a peace offering, and peace offerings are redeemed when a blemish befalls them.
rashi:b3.4: Substitution of its body is not redeemed: as it is written: “Then both it and that for which it is substituted shall be sacred; it shall not be redeemed.”
rashi:b4.1: Substitution of its body takes effect even though it is not fit: such as a blemished animal. What is the reason? Like the tithe, which takes effect upon a blemished animal. And the practical difference is that it is eaten with the sanctity of the tithe: it is not slaughtered in the market and not weighed by the litra.
rashi:b4.2: Substitution of its name takes effect only upon an item that is fit: to become consecrated with full sanctity, like other consecrated animals, upon which [sanctity] does not take effect when their blemish preceded their consecration.
rashi:b5.1: And he asks: Because the Merciful One included with regard to it that it effects substitution of its name, is it diminished, so that it does not take effect upon a blemished animal? All the more so it should be treated more stringently, since it is so stringent that it has substitution of its name.
rashi:b5.2: What it included, it included: and the verse included only something that is fit for a peace offering, as it teaches: “The herd,” to include the eleventh as a peace offering.
rashi:b6.1: From where would this come: that we say so?
rashi:b6.2: A new matter: substitution of its name.
rashi:b6.3: Another version: [the baraita] explained that substitution of its name takes effect only upon an item that is fit, and this is logical, since it was made as stringent as other peace offerings. [The question] “is it diminished?” [concerns] substitution of its body, which a verse was needed to include.
rashi:b6.4: And he answers: Yes, for had it not been written with regard to it, we would say: What it included, it included, etc. And “from where would this come,” that we should say so, since this is not one of the principles by which the Torah is expounded? And still, why was it written? Since it comes to be discussed with a new matter, substitution of its name, you have in it only its novelty; therefore it was necessary to include it. And this is the main [explanation]. For according to the version above there are two difficulties. One: what does it mean by “what it included, it included”? There is no point in establishing it so, for substitution of its name, that it is consecrated, is included from “and all the tithe of the herd and the flock,” and that implies [an animal] without qualification, whether unblemished or blemished; and what it included from “the herd” it included only for sacrifice, so that you should not say we should judge it like substitution of its body. And further, it asks: “From where would this come?” and this is not the Talmud’s language, since it established that it is certainly diminished, for what it did not include, it did not include; it should have said: From where do you have this, that we say so? But according to this version, “from where would this come” is well understood; that is to say: from where does it come to me that we should say so, so that a verse was needed to include it?
rashi:b7.1: Since he accepted it upon himself: to sacrifice it, even though he said: This is [a burnt offering].
rashi:b8.1: Surplus: such as a guilt offering that was consigned to grazing, whose money is brought as a burnt offering; and such as one who set aside money for his sin offering and his guilt offering and some was left over: he brings a burnt offering with that money. For this is the exposition of Jehoiada the priest: Whatever comes from the surplus of a sin offering and from the surplus of a guilt offering, burnt offerings are to be bought with it, the meat to God and the hides to the priests, in the chapter Velad Ḥatat (below, Temurah 23b).
rashi:b9.1: Go to communal gift offerings: to the horn-shaped collection chests.
rashi:b10.1: To an individual gift offering: the owners themselves bring a burnt offering with the money, and it does not count for their obligation; rather, it is as a gift.
rashi:b10.2: Rabbi Eliezer: who holds that surplus goes to an individual gift offering, in the chapter Ve’elu Kodashim (below, Temurah 20b): The substitute of a guilt offering, the offspring of a substitute, their offspring and the offspring of their offspring until the end of the world, shall graze until they become blemished, and they are sold and their money goes to gift offerings, to the horn-shaped chests. Rabbi Eliezer says: He brings a burnt offering with its money.
rashi:b11.1: He agrees with him in one: that surplus goes to an individual gift offering; that is why it was necessary to exclude it from substitution.
rashi:b12.1: If so: that according to Rabbi Shimon a burnt offering of surplus does not effect substitution, then even if he had not substituted for it at first, he could not substitute for it now, for it is a burnt offering that comes from surplus.
rashi:b12.2: And he desacralized it onto another: alternatively, he achieved atonement with another guilt offering, etc., as I explained above in our chapter. [Rashi’s text of the dilemma includes “and he desacralized it onto another,” which the Aramaic printed here lacks; the Davidson English supplies it.]
rashi:b12.3: May he again substitute for it: for where Rabbi Yoḥanan said, according to Rabbi Shimon, that one does not substitute and again substitute, that is where it remains in its sanctity; but, for example, with another sanctity, shall we say that he can substitute, or perhaps there is no difference?
rashi:b13.1: If according to Rabbi Shimon, we derive from the tithe: that is to say, that which Rabbi Shimon derived from the tithe, an item of obligation, to exclude a burnt offering of surplus, which does not effect substitution.
rashi:b14.1: If you find a tanna: who holds like Rabbi Eliezer and like Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said above, according to Rabbi Shimon, that one does not substitute and again substitute, etc.
rashi:b15.1: In two bodies and one sanctity, what: that is, he set aside a guilt offering to achieve atonement with it, and substituted for it, and it became blemished and he desacralized it onto another.
rashi:b16.1: But two sanctities and one body: that is, he achieved atonement with another guilt offering, and the first, lost one was found and was consigned to a burnt offering.
rashi:b16.2: Tiba’ei: the language of the Jerusalem [Talmud], like teiku in the language of the Babylonian [Talmud].
tosafot:b2.1: Rabbi says: Why was the tithe singled out: for Rabbi holds that it was not needed for an individual offering, to exclude the community and partners, since the whole passage of substitution is stated in singular language; and it was also not needed to exclude items consecrated for Temple maintenance, since they are not called an offering; and it was also not needed to exclude a burnt offering of surplus, since he holds that a burnt offering of surplus goes to communal gift offerings, and it is obvious that they do not effect substitution. So Rashi explained. One can further say that he holds that a burnt offering of surplus goes to an individual gift offering, and he holds like Rabbi Eliezer, that it effects substitution.
tosafot:b2.2: To discuss substitution of its body: for it would enter your mind that they do not effect substitution at all, since it was singled out to be discussed with a new matter, as the Talmud explains. Alternatively, “to discuss substitution of its body” means to say that it takes effect upon an item that is not fit. And Rashi explained both.
tosafot:b2.3: Substitution of its name: that is, if he called the tenth ninth, and the ninth tenth, and the eleventh tenth, for we maintain (Bekhorot 60a) that all three are consecrated.
gershom:b1.1: Rabbi Shimon said: But wasn’t the tithe, etc.: for this [“he shall not inquire”] refers to the tithe. [And an item that is not in partnership: as is said in the last chapter of Bekhorot: “Shall be yours,” and not of partnership. Rabbi said: For this the tithe was singled out.]
gershom:b2.1: To be discussed with substitution of its name and substitution of its body: for substitution of its name [of the tithe] is sacrificed and substitution of its body is not sacrificed; and this is [to distinguish between] substitution of its name [and substitution of its body]. Substitution of its name is as explained below: From where [is it derived] that if he called the ninth tenth, and the tenth ninth, and the eleventh tenth, the ninth is eaten in its blemished state, the tenth is tithe, and the eleventh is sacrificed as a peace offering and effects substitution? And from where do we derive that they are consecrated? Since it is written: “All the tithe,” from the inclusion of “all.”
gershom:b3.1: And substitution of its body: that is, its actual substitute [is not sacrificed, since the tithe derives “passing,” “passing” from the firstborn, and with regard to the firstborn it is written: “They are sacred”: they, and not their substitutes. And substitution of its name is redeemed. What is the reason? Because peace offerings are redeemed like other consecrated animals, and the substitution of its name is a peace offering and has the law of peace offerings. Substitution of its body is not redeemed, as it is written of the tithe: “It shall not be redeemed,” and their substitute likewise.] [Similarly,] substitution of its body takes effect upon an item that is not fit for an offering, such as a blemished animal, as it is written: “Nor substitute it, good for bad,” which is a blemished animal. And just as the substitution of the tithe takes effect upon a blemished animal, so too it takes effect upon a harlot’s payment, an animal set aside [for idolatry, and one that was worshipped], for we maintain that wherever a blemish does not disqualify, a matter of sexual transgression or idolatry does not disqualify.
gershom:b4.1: And substitution of its name takes effect only upon an item that is fit: to be sacrificed as a peace offering.
gershom:b5.1: They say: what is this? Because the Merciful One included in the tithe that it has substitution of its name, is this substitution of its name diminished compared with substitution of its body? For substitution of its body takes effect upon an animal with a permanent blemish, and substitution of its name does not take effect upon a permanent blemish.
gershom:b6.1: Yes: certainly [we say]: what it included in substitution of its name, it included, such as that it is sacrificed and redeemed [like peace offerings; and what it did not include, to take effect upon an item that is not fit, it did not include.]
gershom:b7.1: And from where would this come: that we say: what it included it included and what it did not include it did not include? Say that it included it for all matters.
gershom:b8.1: Rav Huna said: because it was singled out to be discussed with a new matter, that substitution of its name is sacrificed and redeemed,] which is not so for substitution of its body; therefore you have in it only its novelty alone.
gershom:b9.1: [It is necessary only: that which he said, “an item that comes as an obligation,” is only to exclude:]
gershom:b10.1: A burnt offering that comes from surplus: such as one who set aside money for his obligation and some of it was left over; that one does not effect substitution. For the Rabbis said that surplus goes to communal gift offerings, and the community does not effect substitution.
gershom:b11.1: And this was consigned: this first one, to a burnt offering, because it was found after atonement; [and that is] a burnt offering that comes from surplus. [That is what he asks.]
gershom:b12.1: Another version: If according to Rabbi Shimon, who said we derive from the tithe, it does not effect even one substitution, for he said: just as the tithe, which comes as an obligation, effects substitution; and a burnt offering that comes from surplus does not come as an obligation.
gershom:b13.1: And this is what he asks: if Rabbi Elazar [the daf reads Rabbi Eliezer] holds like Rabbi Shimon, who says one does not substitute and again substitute, that applies only to one body; in two bodies and one sanctity, what? That is, where he did not achieve atonement [with another].
gershom:b14.1: And two sanctities and one body: that is, where it did not become blemished. What? May he again substitute with one body and a different sanctity? What? Tiba’ei.]
gershom:b15.1: We will return to you, HaKol Memirin.
